Permafrost in Alaska has been degrading, potentially enabling increased carbon dioxide (CO2)
absorption through greater productivity of bristle-pointed iris (Iris setoso) plants and other
vegetation, but also potentially enabling increased CO2 output through greater heterotrophic
respiration (CO2 generated by the activity of soil microorganisms). Hydrologist Yonghong Yi
and her colleagues modeled seasonal changes in net CO2 in Alaska in a landscape grid of 1
square kilometer $(\mathrm{km}2)$ cells and again in a grid of $10 \mathrm{km}2$ cells, which are finer resolutions than
most models of net CO2 have achieved. The researchers concluded that variations in the
landscape affect net CO2 in ways that most models are too coarse to capture.

prompt.text:
Which finding from the researchers’ study, if true, would most directly support the researchers’
conclusion?

content.text:
Lower average heterotrophic respiration rates were found for autumn months when modeled
using a grid of $1 \mathrm{km}2$ cells than when modeled using a grid of $10 \mathrm{km}2$ cells.

When seasonal fluxes in average CO2 absorption and heterotrophic respiration were modeled
using a grid of $1 \mathrm{km}2$ cells, much more data were generated than when seasonal fluxes were
modeled using a grid of $10 \mathrm{km}2$ cells, though the two models reported identical net CO2.

Higher average heterotrophic respiration rates were found for summer months than for winter
months when modeled using either a grid of $1 \mathrm{km}2$ cells or a grid of $10 \mathrm{km}2$ cells.

No correlations between seasonal variations in average heterotrophic respiration and CO2
absorption by I. setosa and other plant species were found when modeled using either a grid of 1
$\mathrm{km}2$ cells or a grid of $10 \mathrm{km}2$ cells.
